title: The potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1–6)
hook: the clay spoils, and the potter makes it again into another vessel

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah said he was too young, and your line was before you were born. Did you take the first small step? Day four hundred seventy-four.

If you've ever tried a pottery class, you know the moment. The wheel is spinning, your hands are wet, and the bowl is rising, actually rising, and you're thinking, I'm good at this. Then one thumb presses a little too hard, and the whole wall wobbles, folds, and collapses into a lump. Your heart sinks. But the teacher doesn't sigh and throw it out. She squashes it back into a ball, wets it, slaps it back on the wheel, and says: again. God once sent Jeremiah to watch exactly that. Not to a temple, not to a palace. To a workshop. Today, the potter's house.
screen: `A POTTERY CLASS.` → `THE BOWL COLLAPSES.` → `AGAIN.` → `GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The word comes to Jeremiah: get up and go down to the potter's house, and there I'll let you hear my words. In the King James Bible: "Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels." The potter in Jeremiah's day worked a pair of stone wheels, the lower one spun with his feet, the upper one shaping the clay. Jeremiah watches. And it goes wrong. "And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it." Marred: spoiled, ruined. And the potter doesn't throw the clay away. He keeps it in his hands and starts again, and makes another vessel, not necessarily the same one. Then God speaks: "Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel." Now, this can sound frightening: God can do whatever he likes with us. And the next verses do warn: if a nation does evil, its future can change. But they also say the opposite: if a nation God has warned turns from its evil, God will relent. The clay's story isn't fixed. That's the hope in it. One more detail. In the very next chapter, God sends Jeremiah to buy a finished, fired clay jar, and smash it in front of the city's leaders. A fired jar can't be reshaped. Soft clay still can. Many Christians hear this as a picture of grace: as long as you're still on the wheel, the potter can start again.
screen: `DOWN TO THE WORKSHOP.` · `THE VESSEL WAS MARRED.` · `HE MADE IT AGAIN, ANOTHER VESSEL.` · `SOFT CLAY CAN STILL CHANGE.` · then, large: `AS THE CLAY IS IN THE POTTER'S HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of one thing you spoiled. Settle, and breathe. A conversation that went wrong. A project you abandoned. A promise you broke. A relationship you bent out of shape. Picture it as clay that collapsed on the wheel. Notice the sinking feeling. Now notice that the clay is still there. It isn't thrown away. What would it look like to start again, not to make the same thing, but another vessel, maybe a better one? Hold that picture. If you pray, you can place it in the potter's hands. The bell holds the time.
The potter's house. Where Jeremiah watched a spoiled pot reshaped into another vessel: soft clay in the potter's hands can always begin again.
Your line: the potter starts again. Today, remake one thing you spoiled: the apology, the restart, the second try. Not perfect. Just back on the wheel. Day four hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Christians often use the image of the potter and the clay in prayer and song, asking God to reshape them, and Jeremiah 18 is read in services focused on repentance and new beginnings.

original.note: Hebrew: potter, one who forms. the same root as formed in Genesis 2:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: God is the potter, so he can do whatever he wants to us.
what it means: the potter doesn't throw spoiled clay away. he makes it again, and the clay's future can still change.
what a scholar hears: yotser, potter, shares the root of yatsar, formed, used when God shapes the first human. ancient potters often used paired stone wheels.

notes: 'The wheels' (ovnayim, a dual form) is commonly explained as a pair of stone wheels, the lower kicked by the feet. Confirm.
Yotser (potter) and yatsar (formed) share the root y-ts-r. Confirm.
The reading of 18:7–10 (God relents if a nation turns) presented alongside the warning. Confirm balanced.
Chapter 19's smashing of a fired jar used as a contrast; confirm fair to the text.
